people.label: Sidney Gottlieb
people.sub: Chief, Technical Services Staff Chemical Division 1955; Deputy Chief, Technical Services Division 1963; Chief of TSD, and the officer whose verbal order destroyed the MKULTRA records, January 1973
people.narrative: Sidney Gottlieb is the officer at the centre of the destruction event the board's own MKULTRA hearing node argues from, and three separate opened documents give him three offices in sequence. In March and June 1955 he certifies the invoices of a numbered MKULTRA subproject as Chief of the Chemical Division of the Technical Services Staff, which is the closest thing in the released record to a signature on the money. people.narrative: Groves is the hinge the board has been carrying in prose. The Armed Forces Special Weapons Project node already reproduces the sentence that makes him its first Chief, and the man himself has had no node on a 1,027-node board. The Defense Threat Reduction Agency's own history dates the appointment to 28 February 1947, one year exactly before his retirement on 29 February 1948, with promotion to Lieutenant General on 24 January 1948 while in post. people.label: Harry S. Truman
people.sub: President of the United States from 12 April 1945; signatory of the 22 January 1946 intelligence directive and of the National Security Act of 1947
people.narrative: The president who signed the founding instruments of the structure this board maps has had no node on it, because the board's prose says 'Truman' and never 'Harry'. Two records settle the office and the instruments. The directive of 22 January 1946 creates the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group and the post of Director of Central Intelligence, and carries his signature. The National Security Act of 1947, approved 26 July 1947, creates the National Security Council, the Central Intelligence Agency, the National Military Establishment and a Research and Development Board, and requires the Secretary of Defense to come from civilian life. He is here for the instruments, not for anything said about him on a podcast.

claims.text: The 22 January 1946 directive is signed by him and creates the office by fiat: 'It is my desire, and I hereby direct, that all Federal foreign intelligence activities be planned, developed and coordinated so as to assure the most effective accomplishment of the intelligence mission related to the national security.' The Director of Central Intelligence 'shall be designated by me'.

claims.text: The same directive draws the domestic line the board's later argument keeps testing: 'No police, law enforcement or internal security functions shall be exercised under this directive', and it makes the Authority and the Director 'responsible for fully protecting intelligence sources and methods'.

claims.text: The statute approved on 26 July 1947 creates, in one instrument, the Council, the Agency and the military establishment: 'There is hereby established a council to be known as the National Security Council'; 'There is hereby established under the National Security Council a Central Intelligence Agency with a Director of Central Intelligence, who shall be the head thereof'; 'There is hereby established the National Military Establishment, and the Secretary of Defense shall be the head thereof.'

claims.text: Section 102(d)(5) of the same Act is the residual authority every later covert-action directive is written under: the Agency is 'to perform such other functions and duties related to intelligence affecting the national security as the National Security Council may from time to time direct.'

people.label: Neil H. McElroy
people.sub: Secretary of Defense from 9 October 1957; issued DoD Directive 5105.15 establishing ARPA, 7 February 1958
people.narrative: The board's DARPA node argues a counterfactual about the agency and carries no founding record at all. This is that record and the officer behind it. McElroy was sworn in as Secretary of Defense on 9 October 1957, five days after Sputnik, and on 7 February 1958 issued DoD Directive 5105.15, which established the Advanced Research Projects Agency in the Office of the Secretary of Defense under the authority of the National Security Act of 1947 as amended and Reorganization Plan No. 6 of 1953. The agency's own commissioned history reproduces the directive in full and records that he took a personal hand in the founding and selected Roy W. Johnson as first Director. His public description of the plan predates the name: testifying on 20 November 1957 he called it the Special Projects Agency and was told the name was confusable with the Armed Forces Special Weapons Project.

entities.label: Project MKULTRA
entities.sub: CIA umbrella project for research and development of materials to control human behavior; authorized by DCI Dulles 13 April 1953, records destroyed January 1973
entities.desc: MKULTRA is the documented American precedent for everything this board argues about compartmented programmes and their records. It was authorized by the Director of Central Intelligence in April 1953 as a funding mechanism whose normal procedures for project approval, funding and accounting were waived, and it ran through 149 numbered subprojects at universities, foundations, hospitals and prisons that were in most cases not told whose money it was. Its own Inspector General wrote in 1963 that the practice was to keep no records of the planning and approval of test programmes. In January 1973 the surviving files were destroyed on a verbal order. What defeated the destruction was an administrative accident: one branch's Budget and Fiscal Section had sent its finance folders to the Retired Records Center in 1970 in a departure from normal procedure that the Agency itself could not later explain, and those seven boxes were found in 1977 by an employee working a Freedom of Information Act request. The board's own MKULTRA hearing node argues from this programme without carrying it.
entities.tierRationale: Cluster, tier and C/A/D carried from the verifier's draft in research/leads/verified-dannyjones-1.md section 1.

claims.text: The Inspector General's 1963 survey states the programme's purpose: 'The MKULTRA activity is concerned with the research and development of chemical, biological and radiological materials capable of employment in clandestine operations to control human behavior.' It records that 'MKULTRA was authorized by the then Director of Central Intelligence, Mr. Allen W. Dulles, in 1953' and that 'Normal procedures for project approval, funding, and accounting were waived.'
claims.source: Report of Inspection of MKULTRA, memorandum for the Director of Central Intelligence, 26 July 1963, National Security Archive John Marks Collection Box 8, https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/sites/default/files/documents/1963-07-26%20JM%20Box%208%20F2%20MKUltra-IG_Report-ocr.pdf

claims.text: The same survey records the programme's own record-keeping practice: 'Present practice is to maintain no records of the planning and approval of test programs.' The Director of Central Intelligence quoted that sentence back to the Senate in 1977 as part of the reason so little was known even before the files were destroyed.
claims.source: Report of Inspection of MKULTRA, 26 July 1963, p. 14, quoted in the prepared statement of Admiral Stansfield Turner, Project MKULTRA joint hearing, 3 August 1977, https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/sites/default/files/hearings/95mkultra.pdf

claims.text: The Church Committee text reprinted in the hearing print records the destruction and the chain behind it: 'In January 1973, MKULTRA records were destroyed by Technical Services Division personnel acting on the verbal orders of Dr. Sidney Gottlieb, Chief of TSD. Dr. Gottlieb has testified, and former Director Helms has confirmed, that in ordering the records destroyed, Dr. Gottlieb was carrying out the verbal order of then DCI Helms.'
claims.source: Project MKULTRA, The CIA's Program of Research in Behavioral Modification, joint hearing, 3 August 1977, Appendix B, https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/sites/default/files/hearings/95mkultra.pdf

claims.text: The surviving records are finance folders and they survived by accident. DCI Stansfield Turner reported 'our recent discovery of seven boxes of documents related to Project MKULTRA', found at the Retired Records Center because the Budget and Fiscal Section had sent them there in 1970 in what the statement calls a departure from normal procedure whose reason 'is not known'. As a result 'the material escaped retrieval and destruction in 1973 ... as well as discovery in 1975'.
claims.source: Prepared statement of Admiral Stansfield Turner, Project MKULTRA joint hearing, 3 August 1977, https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/sites/default/files/hearings/95mkultra.pdf

claims.text: The recovered material covers 149 numbered subprojects plus two boxes of audit reports and financial statements from cut-out funding mechanisms and 33 further subprojects unrelated to behavioural work. Turner told the committee the new identities were 'the names of 185 nongovernment researchers and assistants' and 'names of 80 institutions', comprising 44 colleges or universities, 15 research foundations or chemical or pharmaceutical companies, 12 hospitals or clinics and 3 penal institutions. The hearing's own opening statement gives a different figure, 'Eighty-six universities or institutions were involved.'
claims.source: Project MKULTRA joint hearing, 3 August 1977, opening statement and testimony of Admiral Turner, https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/sites/default/files/hearings/95mkultra.pdf

claims.text: On the Danny Jones Podcast, episode 330, 8 September 2025, at 0:23:00 to 0:23:52, Rebecca Lemov described MK-Ultra as run by Sidney Gottlieb from 1953, with about 149 subprojects in the surviving records, officially discontinued in 1963 or 1964. entities.label: Project BLUEBIRD
entities.sub: CIA interrogation-team programme using polygraph, drugs and hypnotism; proposed to the DCI 5 April 1950 outside the Projects Review Committee; renamed ARTICHOKE August 1951
entities.desc: BLUEBIRD is the documented origin of the CIA's behavioural-control work and the earliest instance on this board of a compartment created by deliberately going round the body that reviews compartments. On 5 April 1950 the Chief of the Inspection and Security Staff submitted it directly to the Director of Central Intelligence rather than through the Projects Review Committee, in writing, on the stated ground of the project's sensitivity and covert nature, and asked that knowledge of it be held to the absolute minimum number of persons. What it bought was two interrogation teams of a psychiatrist, a hypnotist and a technician, working under polygraph cover, with a Washington doctor's office as cover for training and experimentation in drugs and hypnotism, for $65,515 a year. It was renamed ARTICHOKE in August 1951 and passed in 1952 from an intelligence unit to an operating one. By July 1952 the Security Office was reporting to the Director that two suspected Russian double agents had been interrogated under a psychiatric-medical cover using narcosis and hypnosis, one of them left with a total amnesia produced by post-hypnotic suggestion.

claims.text: The founding proposal names its own irregularity: 'In view of the extreme sensitivity of this project and its covert nature, it is deemed advisable to submit this project directly to you, rather than through the channel of the Projects Review Committee. Knowledge of this project should be restricted to the absolute minimum number of persons.'
claims.source: Chief, Inspection and Security Staff, CIA, to the Director of Central Intelligence, 'Project Bluebird', Top Secret, 5 April 1950, CIA-RDP83-01042R000800010003-1, National Security Archive John Marks Collection Box 9, https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/sites/default/files/documents/1950-04-05%20JM%20Box%209%20F5%20Replacement%20CIA%20FOIA-ocr.pdf

claims.text: Its purpose, in the document: 'The purpose of this project is to provide for the immediate establishment of interrogation teams for the operational support of OSO and OPC activities. The teams will utilize the polygraph, drugs, and hypnotism to attain the greatest results in interrogation techniques.' A team is a doctor-psychiatrist, a polygraph-hypnotist and a technician, and the doctors' Washington office is to 'serve as a cover for training, experimentation, and indoctrination purposes in the use of drugs and hypnotism'.
claims.source: Project Bluebird, 5 April 1950, https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/sites/default/files/documents/1950-04-05%20JM%20Box%209%20F5%20Replacement%20CIA%20FOIA-ocr.pdf

claims.text: The one-year budget in the attachment totals $65,515.00: $40,800 personnel, $1,025 supplies, $3,190 equipment, $18,000 transportation and $2,500 rent, itemised down to a Keeler polygraph machine and its spare part kit.
claims.source: Project Bluebird, Attachment A, 5 April 1950, https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/sites/default/files/documents/1950-04-05%20JM%20Box%209%20F5%20Replacement%20CIA%20FOIA-ocr.pdf

claims.text: The programme's lineage is in the 1977 Senate print: 'The earliest of the CIA's major programs involving the use of chemical and biological agents, Project BLUEBIRD, was approved by the Director in 1950 ... In August 1951, the project was renamed ARTICHOKE.' Responsibility passed in 1952 from the Office of Scientific Intelligence to the Inspection and Security Office, which the same text reads as a shift from studying hostile powers to using the techniques.
claims.source: Project MKULTRA joint hearing, 3 August 1977, Appendix B, section 2, https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/sites/default/files/hearings/95mkultra.pdf

claims.text: By July 1952 the Security Office was reporting operational use to the Director: '(a) Subjects were Russian agents suspected of being doubled. (b) Cover was psychiatric-medical. (c) Control methods were by narcosis, by hypnosis, and by combination of both.' The attachment records one interrogation held for about an hour and forty minutes 'with a subsequent total amnesia produced by post-hypnotic suggestion'.
claims.source: Memorandum for the Director of Central Intelligence, 'Successful Application of Narco-Hypnotic Interrogation (ARTICHOKE)', CIA Security Office, July 1952, National Security Archive John Marks Collection Box 6, https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/sites/default/files/documents/1952-07-14%20JM%20Box%206%20F13%20Artichoke-ocr.pdf

entities.label: John Marks FOIA request F-76-374 and the recovery of the MKULTRA finance file
entities.sub: The FOIA request and litigation that caused CIA to search the Retired Records Center in 1977 and find seven boxes the 1973 destruction order had missed
entities.desc: This is the board's own argument about custody, documented, in another programme. A destruction order given inside CIA in January 1973 removed the MKULTRA files; two Senate committees investigating in 1975 could not recover them; and what defeated the order was a single Freedom of Information Act request and the litigation behind it. The Agency's own memorandum of 22 June 1977 says so in one sentence: as a result of John Marks's FOIA request F-76-374, the Office of Technical Service reviewed its holdings and then searched the Retired Records Center, and it was in that second search that the subproject files were found among the retired records of the Budget and Fiscal Section. Among them was the original memorandum setting up MKULTRA over Allen Dulles's signature. The record also corrects the popular account of the sequence: the finding was done by CIA staff, the Agency was advised to tell the Senate Select Committee before it told the requester's attorneys, and the material reached the public through a Senate hearing six weeks later. The collection those documents sit in today carries his name.
entities.tierRationale: Cluster, tier and C/A/D carried from the verifier's draft in research/leads/verified-dannyjones-1.md section 5.

claims.text: The Agency's own memorandum names the request and the mechanism: 'As a result of John Marks FOIA request (F-76-374), all of the MKULTRA material in OTS possession was reviewed for possible release to him. Following that review, the OTS material in the Retired Records Center was searched. It was during that latter search that the subproject files were located among the retired records of the OTS Budget and Fiscal Section.'
claims.source: Memorandum for the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence, 'Request for Guidance on Handling Recently Located MKULTRA Material', 22 June 1977, David S. Brandwein, Director, Office of Technical Service, Appendix B of the Project MKULTRA joint hearing, https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/sites/default/files/hearings/95mkultra.pdf

claims.text: The same memorandum records that the case was in litigation and sets the order of notification: 'The MARKS case is in litigation and we are committed to advise Mr. Marks of the existence of these files shortly, and to deliver the releasable material to his attorneys by 31 July.' Its recommended actions are to release sanitized material to his attorneys as required by FOIA litigation and to 'Inform the Senate Select Committee of the existence of the recently located records prior to informing Mr. Marks' attorneys.'
claims.source: Memorandum for the DDCI, 22 June 1977, Appendix B of the Project MKULTRA joint hearing, https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/sites/default/files/hearings/95mkultra.pdf

claims.text: The Senate said the same thing without the name: 'Then one individual, through a Freedom of Information request, accomplished what two U.S. Senate committees could not. He spurred the agency into finding additional records pertaining to the CIA's program of experimentation with human subjects.'
claims.source: Opening statement, Project MKULTRA joint hearing, 3 August 1977, https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/sites/default/files/hearings/95mkultra.pdf

claims.text: The recovered boxes included the programme's founding paper. The 22 June 1977 memorandum notes that 'the original memorandum setting up MKULTRA, signed [by] Mr. Dulles, is also among these documents.'
claims.source: Memorandum for the DDCI, 22 June 1977, Appendix B of the Project MKULTRA joint hearing, https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/sites/default/files/hearings/95mkultra.pdf

entities.label: Death of Frank R. Olson, 1953, and the compensation and litigation that followed
entities.sub: Army civilian dosed with LSD without his knowledge at a CIA meeting on 19 November 1953; died in New York days later; compensated by Private Law 94-126 in 1976; the family's 2012 suit dismissed in D.D.C. in 2013
entities.desc: This is the one death inside a compartmented American programme that the government conceded, compensated by statute, and then litigated over sixty years later, and it belongs on this board because the paper trail exists on both sides. Frank R. Olson, a civilian employee of the Army at Fort Detrick, was given LSD without his knowledge in a bottle of Cointreau at a CIA and Army meeting on 19 November 1953 and died in New York within about a week. The Rockefeller Commission disclosed the connection in June 1975 without naming him, and attached to its own account a footnote saying the few remaining Agency records indicate he may have had a history of emotional instability. Congress paid his widow and three children $187,500 each in 1976 in exchange for a full waiver, and President Ford signed it saying his administration had wanted twice that. In 2012 two of the children sued the United States alleging the death was a murder concealed for sixty years; the District of Columbia dismissed the suit in 2013 on timeliness, the 1976 waiver and sovereign immunity, while recording that the public record supports many of the allegations. Four opened records disagree about which floor he fell from, what day he died and whether anyone was reprimanded.
entities.tierRationale: Cluster, tier and C/A/D carried from the verifier's draft in research/leads/verified-dannyjones-1.md section 6.

claims.text: The Rockefeller Commission's June 1975 report disclosed the death without naming him: 'on one occasion during the early phases of this program (in 1953), LSD was administered to an employee of the Department of the Army without his knowledge ... Several days later, he jumped from a tenth floor window of his room and died as a result.' Its footnote to that passage reads: 'There are indications in the few remaining Agency records that this individual may have had a history of emotional instability.'
claims.source: Report to the President by the Commission on CIA Activities within the United States, June 1975, chapter 16, pp. 227-228, https://documents2.theblackvault.com/documents/rockefellercommissionreport-full.pdf

claims.text: The same report records the ruling that produced death benefits and the discipline that followed: 'The General Counsel ruled that the death resulted from "circumstances arising out of an experiment undertaken in the course of his official duties for the United States Government," thus ensuring his survivors of receiving certain death benefits. Reprimands were issued by the Director of Central Intelligence to two CIA employees responsible for the incident.' The 2012 complaint states the opposite on the second point, that the internal investigation issued no formal reprimands.
claims.source: Report to the President by the Commission on CIA Activities within the United States, June 1975, p. 227, https://documents2.theblackvault.com/documents/rockefellercommissionreport-full.pdf

claims.text: Congress compensated the family by private statute. Private Law 94-126, 90 Stat. 3006 (1976), directs payment of 'the sum of $187,500 each to Alice W. Olson, Lisa Olson Hayward, Eric Olson, and Nils Olson, in full settlement of all of their claims against the United States arising out of the death of Doctor Frank R. Olson in November 1953, if all of them waive any and all rights arising out of such death.'
claims.source: Private Law 94-126, 90 Stat. 3006 (1976), quoted in full in Olson v. United States, No. 12-1924 (JEB), D.D.C., memorandum opinion of 17 July 2013, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-dcd-1_12-cv-01924/pdf/USCOURTS-dcd-1_12-cv-01924-0.pdf

claims.text: President Ford signed the bill on 12 October 1976 and stated the administration's own position on the amount: 'Legislation to appropriate $1,250,000 to compensate the wife and three children of Dr. Olson for his death was supported by this administration. However, the Congress approved a measure calling for the payment of a total of $750,000 to these survivors.'
claims.source: Gerald R. Ford, Statement on Signing the Bill Providing for the Relief of the Survivors of Dr. Frank R. Olson, 12 October 1976, https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/statement-signing-the-bill-providing-for-the-relief-the-survivors-dr-frank-r-olson

claims.text: The 2012 suit was brought in the District of Columbia, not Maryland, and was dismissed in 2013 without reaching the merits: 'Concluding that most of the allegations are both untimely and waived by a prior settlement agreement, and that any timely or preserved claims fall outside of the United States' waiver of sovereign immunity, the Court will grant the Government's Motion.' The same opinion records that 'the skeptical reader may wish to know that the public record supports many of the allegations that follow, farfetched as they may sound.'
claims.source: Eric Olson and Nils Olson v. United States of America, Civil Action No. 12-1924 (JEB), United States District Court for the District of Columbia, memorandum opinion filed 17 July 2013, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-dcd-1_12-cv-01924/pdf/USCOURTS-dcd-1_12-cv-01924-0.pdf

claims.text: The four opened records do not agree. The Rockefeller Commission and President Ford give a tenth floor window; the Church Committee text in the 1977 Senate print gives a tenth story window of the Statler Hotel and the death as 27 November 1953; Ford and the 2012 complaint give 28 November; the complaint gives thirteen stories at 2:30 a.m. The CIA told the Senate in 1977 that he 'leaped to his death from a hotel room window in New York City about a week after having unwittingly consumed LSD'.
claims.source: Project MKULTRA joint hearing, 3 August 1977 (Turner statement and Appendix B); Rockefeller Commission report, June 1975; Ford signing statement, 12 October 1976; Olson v. United States, D.D.C., 17 July 2013, https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/sites/default/files/hearings/95mkultra.pdf

entities.label: Project AZORIAN and the Hughes Glomar Explorer

entities.label: CIA Office of Policy Coordination
entities.sub: Covert action office chartered by NSC 10/2 as the Office of Special Projects, 18 June 1948; operating from 1 September 1948
entities.desc: The office the Danny Jones corpus keeps invoking has a charter, and the charter is openable. NSC 10/2 of 18 June 1948 created it inside the Central Intelligence Agency under the residual authority of section 102(d)(5) of the National Security Act of 1947, to plan and conduct covert operations, with its Chief nominated by the Secretary of State, reporting directly to the Director of Central Intelligence, and operating 'independently of other components of Central Intelligence Agency'. Two things a node must say and the transcript does not. The directive names the office the Office of Special Projects; the name Office of Policy Coordination appears only from September 1948, when Frank G. Wisner became Assistant Director for Policy Coordination. And the directive's own definition of covert operations is a definition of deniability rather than of psychological warfare: operations 'so planned and executed that any US Government responsibility for them is not evident to unauthorized persons and that if uncovered the US Government can plausibly disclaim any responsibility for them'.
entities.tierRationale: Cluster, tier and C/A/D carried from the verifier's draft in research/leads/verified-dannyjones-3.md section 4.

claims.text: The charter creates the office by that name: 'A new Office of Special Projects shall be created within the Central Intelligence Agency to plan and conduct covert operations; and in coordination with the Joint Chiefs of Staff to plan and prepare for the conduct of such operations in wartime.'
claims.source: NSC 10/2, National Security Council Directive on Office of Special Projects, 18 June 1948, FRUS 1945-1950, Emergence of the Intelligence Establishment, Document 292, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1945-50Intel/d292

claims.text: It is written under the residual clause of the 1947 Act: the Council directs the creation 'under the authority of Section 102(d)(5) of the National Security Act of 1947'.
claims.source: NSC 10/2, 18 June 1948, FRUS 1945-1950, Emergence of the Intelligence Establishment, Document 292, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1945-50Intel/d292

claims.text: The definition is a definition of deniability. Covert operations are those 'so planned and executed that any US Government responsibility for them is not evident to unauthorized persons and that if uncovered the US Government can plausibly disclaim any responsibility for them', and the named categories are 'propaganda, economic warfare; preventive direct action, including sabotage, anti-sabotage, demolition and evacuation measures; subversion against hostile states'. Espionage, counter-espionage and 'cover and deception for military operations' are expressly excluded.
claims.source: NSC 10/2, 18 June 1948, paragraph 5, FRUS 1945-1950, Emergence of the Intelligence Establishment, Document 292, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1945-50Intel/d292

claims.text: The office was built to sit apart inside its own agency: 'The Chief of the Office of Special Projects shall report directly to the Director of Central Intelligence. For purposes of security and of flexibility of operations, and to the maximum degree consistent with efficiency, the Office of Special Projects shall operate independently of other components of Central Intelligence Agency.'
claims.source: NSC 10/2, 18 June 1948, paragraph 3.c, FRUS 1945-1950, Emergence of the Intelligence Establishment, Document 292, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1945-50Intel/d292

claims.text: The operating name and the first officer come from the same volume's list of persons: 'Wisner, Frank G., Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for the Occupied Areas, 1947-1948; Assistant Director for Policy Coordination, Central Intelligence Agency, from September 1, 1948.' George F. Kennan and John Magruder are recorded as senior consultants to the Office of Policy Coordination representing the Secretary of State and the Secretary of Defense respectively, both from September 1948.

entities.label: U.S. Naval Ordnance Laboratory (White Oak, Silver Spring)
entities.sub: Navy laboratory at White Oak, Silver Spring, where Buehler and Wiley developed the 55-Nitinol shape-memory alloys
entities.desc: The U.S. Naval Ordnance Laboratory at Silver Spring, Maryland is where William J. Buehler and Raymond C. Wiley developed the nickel-titanium shape-memory alloys named 55-Nitinol, the acronym standing for Nickel Titanium Naval Ordnance Laboratory. It reaches this board because the board's strongest materials claim runs the other way: an allegation, carried at Tier 2 on the Battelle node, that the alloy's research lineage is a set of missing 1948-49 Wright-Patterson-sponsored Battelle reports. Two federal reports opened for this pass, one of them written by Battelle for NASA, place the discovery at NOL around 1959 to 1962, cite no NOL nitinol report before August 1961, and cite no Battelle nickel-titanium work before 1968. The Danny Jones corpus dates the NOL discovery to 1954; the record does not support that either.
entities.tierRationale: Cluster, tier and C, A and D reasoned by this build; the draft in research/leads/verified-dannyjones-4.md section 3 carried none. C 1 and A 1 because the opened federal literature places the laboratory at the origin of an alloy the board's Roswell-material allegation runs through, and nothing further; D 1 because the laboratory published, NOLTR 61-75 and the patent both being open documents. Tier B on four opened federal records. dateStart is the date of NOLTR 61-75, the earliest NOL nitinol report anything opened here cites.

claims.text: NASA SP-5110, prepared for NASA by Battelle Memorial Institute in 1972, opens: 'Some 10 years ago, Buehler and Wiley of the U.S. Naval Ordnance Laboratory developed a series of engineering alloys that possess a unique mechanical (shape) memory. The generic name of the series of alloys is 55-Nitinol, where Nitinol stands for Nickel Titanium Naval Ordnance Laboratory.'
claims.source: NASA SP-5110, 55-Nitinol: The Alloy With a Memory, C. M. Jackson, H. J. Wagner and R. J. Wasilewski, Battelle Memorial Institute for the NASA Technology Utilization Office, 1972, Chapter 1, p. 1. https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19720022818/downloads/19720022818.pdf

claims.text: The earliest Naval Ordnance Laboratory nitinol report cited anywhere in SP-5110's reference list is NOLTR 61-75 (AD 266607), Buehler and Wiley, 'The Properties of TiNi and Associated Phases', U.S. Naval Ordnance Laboratory, 3 August 1961. The report's own acknowledgments state that 'All the information in the report covers the period from 1955 to March 31, 1970.'
claims.source: NASA SP-5110, references 12 and 74, and Acknowledgments, p. iv. https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19720022818/downloads/19720022818.pdf

claims.text: US Patent 3,174,851, 'Nickel-base alloys', by William J. Buehler and Raymond C. Wiley, assigned to the United States as represented by the Secretary of the Navy, was filed on 1 December 1961 and granted on 23 March 1965.
claims.source: US Patent 3,174,851. https://patents.google.com/patent/US3174851A/en

claims.text: Battelle's documented role in the alloy is late and contractual. NASA CR-1433 of September 1969 records that the nitinol was 'supplied by Mr. William J. Buehler of the Magnetism and Metallurgy Division of the U.S. Naval Ordnance Laboratory (NOL), Silver Spring, Maryland', and that 'As subcontractor to GAC, Battelle Memorial Institute (BMI), Columbus, Ohio, processed the basic Nitinol rod'. The same report calls the NOL work 'the recent discovery'.
claims.source: NASA CR-1433, Nitinol Characterization Study, Goodyear Aerospace Corporation report GER 14188 under contract NAS 1-7522 for NASA Langley Research Center, September 1969, Foreword p. iii and p. 2. https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19690026989/downloads/19690026989.pdf

entities.label: Justification for US Military Intervention in Cuba (Operation Northwoods), 13 March 1962
entities.sub: Joint Chiefs of Staff memorandum to the Secretary of Defense, JCS 1969/321, TOP SECRET SPECIAL HANDLING NOFORN; released through the JFK Assassination Records Review Board
entities.desc: On 13 March 1962 the Joint Chiefs of Staff sent the Secretary of Defense a memorandum forwarding a set of fabricated pretexts that would justify American military intervention in Cuba, and the Chairman, Gen. L. L. Lemnitzer, signed it. Its annex is headed 'PRETEXTS TO JUSTIFY US MILITARY INTERVENTION IN CUBA' and proposes, among other courses of action, blowing up a US ship in Guantanamo Bay and blaming Cuba, and substituting a duplicate aircraft at Eglin Air Force Base for a civil airliner belonging to a CIA proprietary company so that its apparent destruction could be attributed to Cuba. The board argues that cover stories are constructed deliberately at institutional level; this is the declassified instance of exactly that, drafted, staffed and signed at the top of the military chain, and released only because a records statute reached it in 1997. It belongs on the board as a document, not as an assertion about any other case.

claims.text: The Chairman signed it and the Joint Chiefs asked for the mission. The signature block reads 'For the Joint Chiefs of Staff / L. L. LEMNITZER / Chairman / Joint Chiefs of Staff', and paragraph 3 states: 'It is recommended that this responsibility for both overt and covert military operations be assigned the Joint Chiefs of Staff.'
claims.source: Memorandum for the Secretary of Defense, Justification for US Military Intervention in Cuba (TS), 13 March 1962, JCS 1969/321, https://archive.org/download/OperationNorthwoods/operation_northwoods_djvu.txt

claims.text: The annex names itself: 'ANNEX TO APPENDIX TO ENCLOSURE A / PRETEXTS TO JUSTIFY US MILITARY INTERVENTION IN CUBA', and its first course of action states the method in the document's own words: 'Since it would seem desirable to use legitimate provocation as the basis for US military intervention in Cuba a cover and deception plan ... could be executed as an initial effort to provoke Cuban reactions.'
claims.source: Annex to Appendix to Enclosure A, 13 March 1962, https://archive.org/download/OperationNorthwoods/operation_northwoods_djvu.txt

claims.text: One proposed pretext was a staged attack on American forces: 'A "Remember the Maine" incident could be arranged in several forms: a. We could blow up a US ship in Guantanamo Bay and blame Cuba.'
claims.source: Annex to Appendix to Enclosure A, paragraph 3, 13 March 1962, https://archive.org/download/OperationNorthwoods/operation_northwoods_djvu.txt

claims.text: Another named a specific base and a specific cover organisation: 'An aircraft at Eglin AFB would be painted and numbered as an exact duplicate for a civil registered aircraft belonging to a CIA proprietary organization in the Miami area.'
claims.source: Annex to Appendix to Enclosure A, paragraph 8a, 13 March 1962, https://archive.org/download/OperationNorthwoods/operation_northwoods_djvu.txt
